name: Team Rubicon (charityevals' estimate)
beneficiaries_note: Our build: US disaster response, volunteer training and home rebuilding.
summary: Team Rubicon sends veteran-led volunteer crews (Greyshirts) to US disasters to clear debris and roads, muck out flooded homes, tarp roofs and cut fallen trees, trains and recruits them (its Resilience programme), and rebuilds a few homes years after a disaster. All three programmes are modelled for 2024 (the latest audited year: $38.8 million in cash; the audited statements' $74 million adds $35.7 million of donated goods and services, mostly advertising space at rate-card prices, which counts as others' resources): the volunteers' 284,485 hours valued at what the same work would cost to buy (about three-quarters of the result), 16 rebuilt homes and a $1 million rebuilding grant to SBP (about a quarter), and the volunteers' own wellbeing as a side effect (3%). The result, about 0.001 years of healthy life per $1,000 (0.0003 to 0.006), is under a hundredth of the median global-health charity on the site because the help goes to US households, whose consumption the site's log-income scale makes a dollar do little for, and because the cash cost per volunteer hour (about $140) is several times the value of the hour's work. Every branch is discounted for missing data: Team Rubicon counts hours and homes but not the households served or the value of the work to them. The biggest uncertainties are what the work is worth to those served and what others would have done for them anyway.

source.title: charityevals' estimate: Team Rubicon's disaster response, volunteer training and home rebuilding (2024)

sections.title: Other outcomes, in this model's unit
sections.explainer: charityevals' standard step for outcomes in more than one unit (docs/normalization.md 2.6): each outcome is counted in its own unit (units of value for income and deaths, WELLBYs for life satisfaction, tonnes of CO₂e, chicken pain days) and put into this model's unit by its unit's conversion over this unit's, which the headline's conversion cancels. So each moves only with its own sliders, exactly as in a model of its own unit. The rows are fixed; don't edit them.

rows.explainer: What Team Rubicon spent on its programmes in 2024 without donated services (the Form 990's figures): Response $19.29 million, Resiliency $4.16 million and Rebuild (long-term recovery) $3.77 million. The audited statements book $61.14 million of programme expenses because they include $35.66 million of donated goods and services at their stated value, $30.89 million of it advertising space donated to the Resilience programme at 'standard bill rates' (audited statements, note 10); the Form 990 leaves donated services out but keeps donated goods ($1.06 million of supplies). Its totals reconcile to the audited ones: $74,351,135 less $35,664,829 is $38,686,306, against the 990's $38,818,406. A donor's dollar buys this work; the donated services are others' resources and lower Team Rubicon's credit (attribution_share_shared), as Convention 2 asks. All three programmes are modelled here, as branches: Response (disaster response, recovery and mitigation operations, the one 'humanitarian' operation and local service projects), Resilience (training and recruiting volunteers, whose result is the Response work), and Rebuild.

source.quote: our Greyshirts donated 284,485 volunteer hours and delivered a stunning $11,149,821 of volunteer labor to communities large and small

rows.explainer: Hours Greyshirts gave on disaster operations, mitigation, local service projects and the rebuild programme in 2024, Team Rubicon's own count (Form 990 Schedule O gives the same figures: 284,485 hours and $11,149,821 of volunteer labour).

rows.label: Share of the hours spent working for the people and places served
rows.explainer: Our judgment: part of the volunteer hours goes to travel, check-in, standby, base-camp logistics and supervision, and part of the 902 service projects is work for organisations (food banks, cemeteries, scout camps, trails) rather than for disaster-hit households. Team Rubicon counts all of it as labour delivered, and doesn't say whether training time (nearly 30,000 trainings, many during operations: annual report pp. 22-23) is logged as hours. The work for organisations' clients is in unmodelled_benefits_adj. 75%, from 45% to 90%.

rows.label: Volunteer hours per household served
rows.explainer: Our judgment, to turn hours into households (the log-income gain below depends on it only weakly, since the value is spread over them): mucking out a flooded house takes a strike team of 5 to 8 a day or two (40 to 130 hours), tarping a roof or removing a fallen tree a few hours to a day for a crew (10 to 30 hours), and route clearance serves whole streets. Team Rubicon publishes no count of homes or work orders. 45 hours, from 20 to 100.

rows.label: Households served by response, recovery and mitigation work, 2024
rows.explainer: The hours worked for those served over the hours a household takes: about 4,700 households.

rows.explainer: Team Rubicon's one grant of the year, inside the Rebuild programme's $3.77 million: SBP rebuilds disaster-damaged homes with volunteers and AmeriCorps members.

rows.label: Full cost of an SBP home rebuild
rows.explainer: Our judgment: SBP's rebuilds use volunteers and AmeriCorps members, so their cost is below Team Rubicon's own cash spending per home (about $173,000: Rebuild's $3,765,066 less the $1 million grant, over 16 homes, with workforce training and programme staff in the same line), but a disaster rebuild of a damaged house still runs to tens of thousands of dollars in materials and trades. $75,000, from $40,000 to $150,000.

rows.label: Homes rebuilt with the grant (home-equivalents)
rows.explainer: The grant over the full cost of a home: the share of SBP's homes the grant paid for.

rows.label: People in those homes
rows.explainer: At the rebuild programme's own people per home (26 in 16).

rows.label: People served, all branches
rows.explainer: Response households, the rebuilt homes and SBP's homes paid for by the grant. Team Rubicon International LLC (income $987,488, Form 990 Schedule R) runs operations abroad, but the 990 reports under $10,000 of programme activity outside the US in 2024 (Part IV lines 14b-16 all 'No'), so no foreign branch is modelled. Team Rubicon's own figure, 'more than 3 million people impacted', counts whole communities served by route clearance and the like, not people helped directly.

rows.label: Cost per person served
rows.explainer: Context: the full cash cost over everyone served directly.

rows.label: Value of a volunteer hour, US, 2024
rows.explainer: The site's US value of a volunteer hour (@united_states.volunteer_hour_value_2024, Independent Sector: the production and non-supervisory wage plus benefits). Team Rubicon's own $11.15 million for 284,485 hours is $39.19 an hour.

rows.label: Response: what the same work would cost to buy, per volunteer hour, as a multiple of that wage
rows.explainer: Our judgment, as the product of two parts: what a household would pay a contractor per worker-hour for the same debris removal, muck-out, tree work or tarping, as a multiple of the production wage with benefits (equipment, insurance, overhead and margin: 1.5 to 2.5 times it, best 2), times how much of a professional's work a volunteer crew does in an hour (0.6 to 0.8, best 0.7; trained sawyers, heavy-equipment operators and leaders do more). The product is 1.4, from 0.9 to 2.0. Neither part has a published source for this work; both are judgments.

rows.label: Response: what the work is worth to those served, per dollar of its price
rows.explainer: Our judgment: help in kind is worth less to people than its price in cash, since some would not have bought all of it; the same question as Habitat for Humanity's models' in-kind value (0.8, after Olsen 2003 on US housing assistance). Urgent clean-up is close to what people need most, but some of it (yard debris, extra tree work) they would have left. 0.8, from 0.5 to 1.

rows.label: Response: value of the work for those served, 2024
Response: value per person served
rows.explainer: About $1,600 per household, $640 a person at the best guesses.

rows.label: US consumption per person, household survey, 2024
rows.explainer: The site's US consumption per person (@united_states.ce_expenditure_per_person_2024, Consumer Expenditure Survey).

rows.label: The poorest fifth's consumption per person, relative to the average
rows.explainer: The site's anchor for a US social service's clients: the poorest fifth spend 45% of the average household's (BLS 2024), in households of 1.6 people against 2.4, so 0.67 per person.

rows.label: Response clients' consumption relative to the poorest fifth
rows.explainer: Our judgment: Team Rubicon prioritises socially vulnerable places (the communities it served average 0.63 on CDC's Social Vulnerability Index, in the most vulnerable 37%: annual report p. 28) and elderly, disabled and uninsured homeowners, but most of its clients own their homes, which the poorest renters don't. A little above the poorest fifth, as the American Red Cross model's large-disaster clients (1.1): 1.2, from 0.9 to 1.6.

rows.label: Response clients' consumption per person relative to the US average
Response clients' consumption per person a year
Years the response help counts for
rows.explainer: 1: a one-off service counted once at the year's consumption.

rows.label: Response: log-consumption gain per person
rows.formula: resp_inkind_value * ln(1 + resp_value_per_person / baseline_consumption) * pv_annuity_due(1, $discount_rate, income_years)
rows.explainer: The site's one log-income scale at the clients' own consumption.

rows.label: Rebuild: market cost of the rebuild work per home, without the volunteers' labour
rows.explainer: Our judgment: what it would cost the owner to have the house rebuilt or substantially repaired by contractors, leaving out the volunteers' own labour (their hours are in vol_hours and valued in the response branch, so they are not counted twice). Team Rubicon's own cash spending was about $173,000 a home (Rebuild's $3,765,066 less the $1 million grant, over 16 homes), but that includes workforce training and programme staff; a modest rebuilt or gutted-and-restored house of 1,000 to 1,500 square feet costs roughly $100 to $150 a square foot from contractors (about $130,000), of which labour is roughly 30 to 45%; Greyshirts do much of the unskilled and semi-skilled work and local contractors the trades, so about a quarter to a third of the price is taken out. $90,000, from $50,000 to $150,000.

rows.label: Rebuild: years a rebuilt home serves the family
rows.explainer: Our judgment, as in Habitat for Humanity's US model (15 years for owners staying, repairs 10 to 25): a rebuilt house lasts decades, but the owners are often elderly. 25, from 12 to 40. The result moves little with it: the value is spread over the same years it is discounted over.

rows.label: Rebuild: people per home
rows.explainer: Team Rubicon's own count: 26 people in 16 homes.

rows.label: Rebuild clients' consumption relative to the poorest fifth
rows.explainer: Our judgment: the programme rebuilds 'for some of the most at-risk families with the fewest resources to recover' (Form 990 Schedule O), still without a home years after the disaster: about the poorest fifth, 1, from 0.75 to 1.3.

rows.label: Rebuild clients' consumption per person a year
Rebuild: what a rebuilt home is worth to the family, per dollar of its cost
rows.explainer: The same question and value as Habitat for Humanity's US model: US housing assistance is valued by recipients at less than its cost (Olsen 2003). 0.8, from 0.6 to 0.95.

rows.label: Rebuild: log-consumption gain per person
rows.formula: ltr_inkind_value * ln(1 + ltr_value_per_home / ltr_people_per_home / pv_annuity_due(1, $discount_rate, ltr_years) / ltr_baseline) * pv_annuity_due(1, $discount_rate, ltr_years)
rows.explainer: The home's value as an even yearly flow over its years (its present value equals the cost at the shared discount rate), per person, on the log scale at the family's consumption, over those years.

rows.label: SBP homes: log-consumption gain per person
rows.formula: ltr_inkind_value * ln(1 + sbp_cost_per_home / ltr_people_per_home / pv_annuity_due(1, $discount_rate, ltr_years) / ltr_baseline) * pv_annuity_due(1, $discount_rate, ltr_years)
rows.explainer: As for Team Rubicon's own rebuilds, at SBP's full cost per home.

rows.label: Log-consumption gain per person, all branches (for reading)
rows.formula: (resp_people * resp_ln_per_person + ltr_people * ltr_ln_per_person + sbp_people * sbp_ln_per_person) / people_reached
rows.explainer: The branches' gains averaged over everyone served; each branch is adjusted on its own below.

rows.label: Volunteers who deployed on operations, 2024

source.title: Team Rubicon, Inc., Form 990 for 2024 (public disclosure copy, signed 17 November 2025)
source.page: Schedule O, Part III line 4a, p. 45
source.quote: IN 2024 ALONE, NEARLY 6,000 VOLUNTEER GREYSHIRTS COMPLETED 98 OPERATIONS ACROSS 272 COMMUNITIES IN THE U.S.

rows.explainer: 'Nearly 6,000' Greyshirts deployed on the 98 operations; local service projects add others, so up to 9,000.

rows.label: Volunteers' own life satisfaction gained, points for the year
rows.explainer: Our judgment, a side effect on the volunteers (53% veterans, 69% over 55: annual report pp. 35-37): purpose, belonging and skills. Panel studies that match volunteers to similar non-volunteers find regular volunteering raises life satisfaction, mainly among the less happy, and more the longer it lasts (Binder and Freytag 2013, Journal of Economic Psychology 34: 97-119, British Household Panel Survey); the effects are small, and a Greyshirt gives about 47 hours a year (284,485 hours over about 6,000), a week's deployment. 0.05 points (0-10) for the year, from 0 to 0.15.

rows.label: Life satisfaction gained per person served, points a year (volunteers' gain spread over everyone served)
rows.explainer: The volunteers' WELLBYs spread over the people served, so the template's bridge row stays as it is.

rows.label: Years the volunteers' gain lasts
rows.explainer: 1: counted for the year of service.

rows.label: WELLBYs per person served
Health gained other than deaths
rows.explainer: 0: illness averted by mucking out (mould exposure after floods) and injuries averted by route clearance and tarping have no outcome data; they are in unmodelled_benefits_adj.

rows.label: Deaths averted per person
rows.explainer: 0: Team Rubicon's work comes days to months after the emergency, once rescue is over; deaths possibly averted (roads cleared for emergency vehicles) are in unmodelled_benefits_adj.

rows.label: Share of deaths averted under five (not used: no deaths modelled)
rows.explainer: Not used, since deaths_averted_per_person is 0; kept so value_per_death is the site's standard row. About the US share of deaths under five (under 1%).

rows.label: Share 5-14 of deaths over five (not used)
rows.explainer: Not used, since deaths_averted_per_person is 0; kept so value_per_death is the site's standard row. Children 5-14 are about 0.3% of US deaths (CDC), so 1% of deaths over five, from 0 to 5% for disaster deaths that strike children more.

rows.label: Share 15-49 of deaths over fifteen (not used)
rows.explainer: Not used, since deaths_averted_per_person is 0; kept so value_per_death is the site's standard row. Adults 15-49 are about 10% of US deaths over fifteen (CDC); from 5% to 20% for disaster and storm-clean-up deaths, which fall more on working-age men.

rows.label: Value of a death averted (units of value)
rows.explainer: The site's one value of a death, by age band, times your value of a life.

rows.label: Response: units of value before adjustments
Rebuild: units of value before adjustments
SBP grant: units of value before adjustments
Response: trust in the hours and work counted
rows.explainer: Our judgment, validity only: the value is labour at a price (no effect study needed); the hours are Team Rubicon's own count from its volunteer system, not audited. The judged parts (hours per household, price, in-kind value) are rows of their own. 0.9, from 0.75 to 1.

rows.label: Response: share of the work no one else would have done for free
rows.explainer: Our judgment: without Team Rubicon some households would have been helped by other voluntary groups (Samaritan's Purse, Southern Baptist Disaster Relief, Mennonite Disaster Service, SBP, the Crisis Cleanup network's members) or by insurers and FEMA's debris programmes; those who would have paid a contractor themselves count in full (Team Rubicon saved them the price), as do those who would have gone without. After Helene, Milton and the 2024 floods the voluntary groups had long waiting lists. 0.55, from 0.3 to 0.8.

rows.label: Rebuild: trust in the homes counted
rows.explainer: Our judgment: 16 homes completed are a count Team Rubicon could check; the value per home is a judgment of its own row. 0.95, from 0.8 to 1.

rows.label: Rebuild: share of the rebuild that wouldn't have happened anyway
rows.explainer: Our judgment, years brought forward and the counterfactual as one question: the families were still out of their homes years after the disaster (a Harvey survivor rebuilt seven years on: annual report p. 24), after FEMA's capped grants and loans; some would have been rebuilt later by another group or their own means, which counts as part of the value lost. 0.5, from 0.25 to 0.8.

rows.label: SBP grant: share of the homes that wouldn't have been rebuilt anyway
rows.explainer: The same question as Team Rubicon's own rebuilds: SBP serves the same kind of families.

rows.label: SBP grant: share not replaced by SBP's other funders
rows.explainer: Our judgment: SBP raises money from many funders and FEMA-funded state programmes; without Team Rubicon's grant part of the same homes would have been paid for by others. 0.8, from 0.5 to 1.

rows.label: Volunteers: trust in the wellbeing gain
rows.explainer: Our judgment: the volunteering studies are observational (matching on panel data), people who volunteer differ, and a week's deployment is a lighter dose than the regular volunteering studied. 0.5, from 0.2 to 0.8.

rows.label: Volunteers: share who wouldn't have volunteered elsewhere
rows.explainer: Our judgment: many Greyshirts would volunteer with another group (fire departments, other disaster groups, veterans' organisations) without Team Rubicon. 0.5, from 0.2 to 0.8.

rows.label: Partners' resources behind the work, as a share of Team Rubicon's cost
rows.explainer: Our judgment: loaned heavy equipment (CNH and CASE's fleet, annual report p. 44), churches and schools housing volunteers, local governments hauling debris from the curb, and FEMA's and the states' coordination. 10%, from 3% to 25%.

rows.label: Share of the donated advertising's stated value that counts as a resource behind the work
rows.explainer: Our judgment on valuation only: the advertising is valued at the media's standard bill rates (audited statements, note 10), while donated public-service space is mostly unsold inventory and off-peak slots worth a fraction of the rate card. Whatever it serves (recruiting, fundraising, the brand) it is a resource behind the work at its real worth, as the fundraising cash in cost_total is. 30%, from 10% to 60%.

rows.label: Team Rubicon's share of the resources behind the work
rows.formula: cost_total / (cost_total * (1 + partner_resources_share) + vol_hours * vol_hour_value + inkind_ops + inkind_media * media_resource_share)
rows.explainer: Convention 2: Team Rubicon's cash cost over that plus partners' resources, the volunteers' unpaid hours at the US value of a volunteer hour (Team Rubicon pays their travel, food and equipment, which are in its cost), the donated goods and services at their stated value and the advertising at its counted share: about 0.65. Volunteers' time is a large share of what the work takes.

rows.label: Response: Team Rubicon's share of the resources
rows.explainer: The shared figure above.

rows.label: Rebuild: Team Rubicon's share of the resources
rows.explainer: The shared figure above: the rebuilds use the same volunteers, donated materials and partners.

rows.label: SBP grant: Team Rubicon's share of the resources
rows.explainer: 1: the homes counted are the grant's share of SBP's full cost (sbp_homes), volunteers' time included in that cost.

rows.label: Volunteers: Team Rubicon's share of the resources
rows.explainer: The shared figure above: the volunteers' own time is part of what gives them the gain.

rows.label: Response: share of the counted work actually delivered
rows.explainer: Our judgment, for the response branch only: hours logged that did not end in finished work (jobs left part-done when an operation closed, rework). 0.95, from 0.85 to 1. The rebuilt homes are counted as completed, SBP's homes as the grant's share of its cost and the volunteers' gain as theirs, so the other branches take 1.

rows.label: Leverage and funging, Team Rubicon's own work
rows.explainer: Our judgment: no government pays for this work in Team Rubicon's place (it is not a FEMA contractor for it); its operations draw in corporate gifts in kind and volunteers' employers' paid time (Ford's 56 hours: annual report p. 45), a little above 1, and some donors' gifts may replace others'. 1, from 0.9 to 1.05.

rows.label: SBP grant: leverage and funging
Response: missing-data step
rows.explainer: Thin: the hours are Team Rubicon's count, but the households served (hours per household) and the value of the work to them (its price) are judgments, not a measured count of homes and a price paid. So the shared missing-data step (docs/normalization.md 2.12).

rows.label: Rebuild: missing-data step
rows.explainer: Thin: the homes are counted, but their value is a judgment, not the programme's measured cost per home or a valuation.

rows.label: SBP grant: missing-data step
rows.explainer: Thin: the homes the grant paid for are a judgment (SBP's cost per home).

rows.label: Volunteers: missing-data step
rows.explainer: Thin: the effect is a judgment from research on other volunteering.

rows.label: Response: all adjustments
rows.formula: resp_evidence_adj * resp_counterfactual_adj * resp_attribution_share * implementation_adj * leverage_funging_adj * resp_missing_data_adj

rows.label: Rebuild: all adjustments
SBP grant: all adjustments
Volunteers: all adjustments
Evidence (average, for reading)
rows.formula: (resp_uov_raw * resp_evidence_adj + ltr_uov_raw * ltr_evidence_adj + sbp_uov_raw * ltr_evidence_adj) / (resp_uov_raw + ltr_uov_raw + sbp_uov_raw)
rows.explainer: Outcome-weighted average of the income branches, for reading only (Convention 4); each branch applies its own, and the volunteers' branch its own.

rows.label: Counterfactual (average, for reading)
rows.formula: (resp_uov_raw * resp_counterfactual_adj + ltr_uov_raw * ltr_counterfactual_adj + sbp_uov_raw * sbp_counterfactual_adj) / (resp_uov_raw + ltr_uov_raw + sbp_uov_raw)
rows.explainer: Outcome-weighted average of the income branches, for reading only (Convention 4); each branch applies its own, and the volunteers' branch its own.

rows.label: Attribution (average, for reading)
rows.formula: (resp_uov_raw * resp_attribution_share + ltr_uov_raw * ltr_attribution_share + sbp_uov_raw * sbp_attribution_share) / (resp_uov_raw + ltr_uov_raw + sbp_uov_raw)
rows.explainer: Outcome-weighted average of the income branches, for reading only (Convention 4); each branch applies its own, and the volunteers' branch its own.

rows.label: Missing-data step (average, for reading)
rows.formula: (resp_uov_raw * resp_missing_data_adj + ltr_uov_raw * ltr_missing_data_adj + sbp_uov_raw * sbp_missing_data_adj) / (resp_uov_raw + ltr_uov_raw + sbp_uov_raw)
rows.explainer: Outcome-weighted average, for reading only (Convention 4): every branch is thin, so each applies the shared step.

rows.label: All adjustments (average, for reading)
rows.formula: (resp_uov_raw * resp_total_adj + ltr_uov_raw * ltr_total_adj + sbp_uov_raw * sbp_total_adj) / (resp_uov_raw + ltr_uov_raw + sbp_uov_raw)
